div.p: Abstractive summarizers often state facts that are not in the source document. We introduce retrieval-gated decoding (RGD), which blocks a token when no retrieved passage of the source supports it. On the NewsSum-2 benchmark, RGD raises factual consistency from 71% to 84%, while ROUGE-L drops by 0.4 points. We hypothesize that gating at the token level, rather than the sentence level, drives the gain.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Neural abstractive summarization produces fluent text, but a large share of generated summaries contain statements that the source does not support (Maynez et al., 2020). Retrieval-augmented generation reduces this problem for open-domain question answering (Lewis et al., 2020), yet summarizers rarely check each token against the source.
We propose retrieval-gated decoding, which retrieves supporting passages for every candidate token and blocks tokens that no passage supports.

div.head: Method
div.p: At each decoding step, RGD retrieves the top five passages of the source document with BM25 and scores the candidate token against them with an entailment model. A token whose best score falls below a threshold of 0.6 is masked, and the decoder samples among the remaining tokens.

div.head: Experiments
div.p: We evaluate on NewsSum-2, a benchmark of 12,000 news articles with reference summaries, and report factual consistency with the FactCC classifier and ROUGE-L against the references.

div.head: Results
div.p: RGD raises factual consistency from 71% to 84% on NewsSum-2, while ROUGE-L drops by 0.4 points. Gating at the sentence level instead raises factual consistency only to 76%.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We hypothesize that gating at the token level, rather than the sentence level, drives the gain. Whether RGD helps on documents longer than 4,000 tokens remains an open question.
